Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:{ "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a", "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "tags.stratum.phase": "run", "tags.stratum.success": true, "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26, "tags.cpuCount": 8, "tags.memoryInMB": 18000, "tags.diskInMB": 50000, "tags.networkInMbps": 1000, "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1", "ts": 1780743028000}In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:{ "span_id": "38536313f65f060a", "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "phase": "run", "success": true, "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002, "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028, "runtime_secs": 26, "cpu_requested": 8, "memory_mb_requested": 18000, "disk_mb_requested": 50000, "network_mbps_requested": 1000, "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "env": "prod", "resource_usage": }Recommendation GenerationA scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.Figure 4: Recommendation Generation SequenceFor each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:CPU recommendation{ "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU", "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4, "status": 7820.3 }, "execution": { "total_fn_executions": 748762182, "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75, "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723 }, "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" } }, "experiment_inputs": null, "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null, "outcome_message": null, "finalized_at": null}As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.Retry with More ResourcesWe take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.Figure 5: Retry with More ResourcesThis “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.Recommendation VerificationEvery recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.Figure 6: Evaluating StageSynthetic experiment:Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.Typically runs for 1–2 hours.Runs to completion without early termination checks.Figure 7: Synthetic Experiment FlowProduction experiment:Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.Figure 8: Production Experiment FlowThe Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:{ "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7", "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 }, "productionExperiment": { "enabled": true, "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating }}Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:{ "outcome": "APPLIED", "syntheticExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }, "productionExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }}The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.Post-Apply MonitoringPassing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.Figure 9: Unexpected Retries SpikeBecause early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.Figure 10: Recommendation Auto-RevertWe intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.Where Are We TodayOversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.Looking ahead, our key priorities include:Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.CreditsSpecial thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.

title: [Netflix] The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
summary: By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis GarciaIntroductionAny team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.We believe:A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example,A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.”Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build.Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them.What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks.The Lifecycle at a GlanceFigure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them.Figure 1. The four-phase lifecycle of an LLM judge, and the data that flows between the phases.We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset.Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters.In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated.Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases.System componentsFour automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them.Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision.Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement).Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations.Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale.Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out.Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground TruthEverything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later.Why we built our own benchmarkOff-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources:Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces.Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own.Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs.Two details that matteredThe benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale.Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning.Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to HumansThe failure mode: right answer, wrong reasonThere is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance.We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output:a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), anda short natural-language rationale for that label.Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast.The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below.Reasoning-Aligned Rubric TuningWe tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop.Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale.R_i is the current rubric text, y_J(x) the label, and r_J(x) the rationale.At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows.Score the training data with the current rubric.Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop.Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric.The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes:Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s.Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match.So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning.Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses.RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it.Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them.Alignment metricsWe run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics.Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard.Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low.Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason.Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve.Ablation: does the reasoning signal help?To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales.Figure 2. Improvement over the starting rubric, per criterion, for reasoning-aware tuning (RART) and label-only tuning (vanilla).Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t.Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to WorkOnce deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests.Two roles for one judgeOnce we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation:Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails.Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again.The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision.Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serveWe cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served.Figure 3. Cumulative share of explanations that clear the Judge as we allow more revisions, across four generator models.That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget.Do judge-approved explanations help members?Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period.Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful.Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge AlignedA judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop.The weekly human reviewFor each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark.Setting the bar with human disagreementThe panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread.Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We requireso the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt.Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback.What human review catches that metrics can’tBeyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things?In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much.When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references.Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both.Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric.Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members.What We LearnedFive lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge:Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s.Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable.One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once.Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten.Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped.Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making.AcknowledgementsThis post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations.Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Distributed Hybrid Infrastructure
summary: We’re proud to share that Microsoft has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Distributed Hybrid Infrastructure for the fourth consecutive year. Microsoft is positioned highest for Ability to Execute. We believe this recognition reflects the strength of Microsoft’s unified approach to distributed infrastructure. With Azure Local and Azure Arc, organizations can manage infrastructure across datacenters, edge locations, multi-cloud environments, and sovereign deployments through a consistent Azure foundation. Read the full 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Distributed Hybrid Infrastructure report One Azure platform for distributed infrastructure Customers want the flexibility to run workloads where it makes the most sense for their business without taking on additional operational complexity. As infrastructure extends across datacenters, edge locations, and the cloud, Microsoft helps customers maintain consistency through common tools, processes, and management experiences, reducing fragmentation and allowing teams to focus on delivering business value. Azure Arc extends Azure management and governance to resources running in data centers, at the edge, and across multi-cloud environments. Azure Local brings Azure infrastructure and services into customer-controlled locations so organizations can run cloud services and AI workloads closer to their applications and data. Together, Azure Arc and Azure Local give organizations a common way to operate across environments without requiring every workload to run in the same place. Some applications are best suited for the public cloud. Others may need to remain in a corporate data center, operate at the edge, or run within a customer-controlled sovereign environment. While deployment locations differ, management and governance can remain consistent. Microsoft continues to expand the environments Azure Local can support, from small-form-factor edge deployments to large scale data center environments. Azure Local supports both hyperconverged architectures and options for disaggregated compute and external storage, so infrastructure can be designed around the needs of the workload rather than a single deployment model. Choice and operational control for sovereign workloads The same workload-centric approach applies to digital sovereignty, an increasingly important consideration for organizations around the world. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is not a single deployment model, but a continuum of choices and controls. For many workloads, sovereignty requirements can be addressed in public cloud through capabilities for data residency, encryption, confidential computing, policy enforcement, and operational oversight. Other workloads need to run in customer-controlled locations or require greater separation from public cloud operations. Built on Azure Local, Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud supports these scenarios by giving customers greater control over infrastructure, data, operations, and access, while retaining a familiar Azure foundation. For environments where connectivity to the cloud is restricted or unavailable, disconnected operations on Azure Local bring a local control plane into the customer environment. This enables customers to deploy and manage Azure Local and supported capabilities without ongoing connectivity to the cloud. Together, these options allow organizations to apply different levels of sovereignty and operational control to different workloads instead of forcing the entire estate into a single architecture. Bringing AI closer to applications and data The growing adoption of AI is making workload placement decisions even more important. For some workloads, the scale and breadth of the public cloud are the right fit. Others need inference to happen where data is generated because of latency, connectivity, governance, or sovereignty requirements. Foundry Local on Azure Local extends AI inference into Azure Local environments, allowing organizations to deploy and run models closer to their applications and data using Kubernetes-native operations. Investing in what comes next We see the 2026 Gartner recognition as validation of a clear direction: distributed infrastructure should provide customers with choice over where workloads run without requiring fragmented management, governance, and operational models. We will continue investing in connected and disconnected operations, scalable infrastructure, data and AI capabilities, and consistent Azure management across distributed environments. We are grateful for the trust our customers place in us and remain committed to delivering the flexible, consistent, and secure platform they need to power the next generation of distributed infrastructure. title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI agents with HashiCorp Boundary
summary: AI agents are evolving from passive assistants into active participants in enterprise IT operations -analyzing logs, investigating incidents, assessing system health, and recommending next steps. While this can accelerate troubleshooting and reduce operational toil, enterprise adoption requires answering a critical question beyond improving productivity: How can an AI agent interact with infrastructure without creating new security, compliance, or governance risks? This blog explores how to leverage HashiCorp Boundary’s zero trust access model to provide AI agents with secure, governed access to infrastructure resources. To explore this challenge in practice, we used IBM technologies and services to create an AI agent capable of investigating infrastructure incidents through natural-language requests. For example, a platform engineer can ask the agent to analyze a performance issue, gather diagnostic data from a target system, and summarize the findings. The key objective was not only to build an AI agent but to ensure that every infrastructure interaction remained secure, controlled, and auditable. The solution overview The AI agent enables a platform engineer to describe an operational goal in natural language: A sample prompt can be: “Investigate memory pressure on app-server-01 and summarize the findings.” The following diagram shows the architecture and workflow for an AI agent built with IBM Bob. The AI agent uses watsonx and Granite models to interpret an operational request, develop an investigation plan, execute the required diagnostic actions, analyze the results, and produce a concise summary for the platform engineer. When infrastructure access is required, the AI agent initiates a login to Boundary, and the platform engineer completes the authentication on behalf of the agent. The AI agent then opens a Boundary-proxied session to the authorized Linux target to perform the investigation. Session activity is recorded, and audit logs capture authentication events, access decisions, grants, policy changes, and administrative actions. This creates a human-authorized workflow for an AI-assisted operation without relying on fully unattended infrastructure access. The zero trust layer As shown in the architecture diagram, Boundary provides the secure access layer between the AI agent and the target infrastructure. Rather than granting the agent direct access to systems, Boundary evaluates the authenticated user's identity, permissions, and target access policies before establishing a connection. This separation of access control from AI reasoning ensures that infrastructure access remains governed by enterprise security policies. Secure access with Boundary In this model, Boundary enables five essential controls: Identity-based authentication: Boundary delegates authentication to IBM Verify through an OIDC authentication method and applies access policies to the verified identity. Zero trust connectivity: The agent reaches the target only through an active Boundary session, without requiring the agent host to have a direct network route or VPN access to the target’s private network. Boundary workers proxy the connection to the target. Target grants: Least-privilege grants restrict network access to only the Linux targets required for the agent’s operational task. Secrets management: Vault stores or generates target credentials, including short-lived dynamic credentials. Boundary retrieves and injects the credentials when it establishes the session, without returning them to the agent or platform engineer. This ensures credentials are shared, leaked, stolen, or insecurely stored. Administrative control: Authorized administrators can cancel an active session, providing a kill switch for infrastructure access. Auditability and session recording Boundary captures the agent’s infrastructure activity within the same governed access layer used for human operators. Session recordings provide visibility into session interactions and the associated target, user, host, and connection metadata. Boundary also emits audit events for authenticated requests, session activity, and administrative operations. Together, session recording and audit events provide centralized evidence for incident reviews, security investigations, and compliance validation, helping organizations treat the AI agent as a controlled and auditable participant in enterprise operations. Demo The video demonstrates how an AI agent uses a Platform Engineer’s verified identity and permissions to access enterprise resources through Boundary with governance and auditability. Final thoughts As AI agents move from analysis to infrastructure action, enterprises must embed security, governance, and accountability directly into the workflow. Automation alone is not enough; organizations also need controls that govern identity, access, credentials, sessions, and evidence. In this example, we used watsonx.ai to support the agent’s reasoning, planning, and summarization; Boundary to authorize and proxy infrastructure access; Verify to authenticate the platform engineer; and Vault to manage and inject target credentials. Together, these technologies create a secure, governed model for agent-assisted enterprise operations. The agent can help perform infrastructure tasks while operating within the identity, access, session, and audit controls expected from human operators. Building the AI agent You can try testing this workflow out in your environment. There are several possible approaches, but you can build your AI agent and enable secure access to your resources using Boundary by setting up the services and accounts as described below: IBM Cloud and watsonx.ai: Create an IBM Cloud account and use watsonx.ai python SDK to build the agent. IBM watsonx.ai provides access to the foundation models and tools that an AI agent can use for reasoning, planning, and summarization. You can also use IBM Bob, an agentic development partner, to design and implement the AI agent through natural-language prompts. Alternatively, you can use the AI agentic frameworks of your choice to develop your AI agent. Linux host or cloud VM: Create a Linux host in your cloud environment or infrastructure for the agent to inspect. IBM Verify: Sign -up for an Identity Provider (IdP) like IBM Verify. Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) and create a user account. A platform engineer will use this account to authenticate Boundary before the agent opens a session. You can also use other IdPs of your choice. HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) account: Create a free HCP account, deploy Boundary and Vault clusters and complete the following configurations: Configure the Linux host as a Boundary target. Enable session recording for the target and configure an Amazon S3 or supported S3-compatible storage bucket and the applicable storage policies. Store the host credentials in a Boundary static credential store, or, preferably, configure a Vault credential library. Bind the credential source to the SSH target as an injected application credential. Credential injection removes the need for the agent to receive the target credential. Configure Verify as an OIDC authentication provider in Boundary and set the OIDC method as the primary method. Configure Boundary roles and grants to give the authenticated identity least-privilege access to the required target. Local development environment: Install Python and the Boundary CLI on your development machine. The AI agent developed calls watsonx.ai python APIs and connects to the target through a Boundary-proxied session after the platform engineer authenticates. title: [Kubernetes] Spotlight on SIG Apps
summary: As Kubernetes adoption has grown, the conversation has shifted beyond running containers to managing increasingly complex application lifecycles. Modern platforms support stateless web services, stateful databases, batch processing, AI workloads, and platform services. At the same time, they must remain reliable during upgrades, scaling events, and infrastructure failures. Every Kubernetes user relies on SIG Apps, whether they realize it or not. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs form the foundation of how applications are deployed, updated, scaled, and operated across the Kubernetes ecosystem. SIG Apps is focused on improving workload resilience, refining application lifecycle management, and addressing the operational challenges that emerge when applications encounter node failures, rollout disruptions, and increasingly complex infrastructure environments. In this spotlight, we sit down with two of the three SIG Apps chairs Janet Kuo and Maciej Szulik to discuss the evolution of Kubernetes workload management, the challenges of balancing application reliability with operational simplicity, and the future of application lifecycle management within one of Kubernetes’ most influential Special Interest Groups. Introducing SIG AppsNatalie Fisher: Can you introduce yourself, your role, and how you got involved in SIG Apps? Janet Kuo: I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. In those early days, my focus was on building the core Workloads API, specifically developing controllers like Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, and DaemonSet, defining their rollout behaviors, and bringing them from initial designs to GA. That hands-on work was my entry point into SIG Apps. Since then, I've stayed deeply involved in both the technical and community sides of Kubernetes. I have led SIG Apps as Co-Chair and Tech Lead since 2019. Currently, in addition to maintaining the workloads API, I am driving new subprojects like the Agent Sandbox to ensure Kubernetes is ready for next-generation agentic and AI workloads. Maciej Szulik: I started contributing to Kubernetes all the way back in 2014. Since then, I've worked across various areas of the project: controllers, kubectl, and apimachinery, which eventually led me to become one of the Chairs and Tech Leads for SIG Apps. My current focus is reliability of the workload controllers under the SIG Apps umbrella and stability and ease of use of kubectl as part of my SIG CLI Tech Lead role. I also care about overall community health and growth as part of my Steering Committee role. Outside of Kubernetes, I work as a Staff Platform Engineer at Defense Unicorns, where I'm helping make Kubernetes more airgap-native with a project called zarf. The problem and the solutionSIG Apps is responsible for the core workload APIs that power how applications run on Kubernetes. From Deployments and StatefulSets to Jobs and CronJobs, these controllers determine how workloads are created, updated, scaled, and recovered when things go wrong. As Kubernetes expands to support increasingly diverse workloads – including AI, batch processing, and large-scale distributed applications – SIG Apps continues to evolve these APIs while balancing reliability, backward compatibility, and operational simplicity. NF: For readers who may not be familiar, what is SIG Apps, and what role does it play within the broader Kubernetes ecosystem? MS: SIG Apps is the Kubernetes Special Interest Group responsible for the workloads APIs. CronJob and Job help running batch workloads, whereas DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, and StatefulSet serve the majority of other applications. More broadly, SIG Apps owns the layer most developers actually touch day-to-day: the controllers that turn a workload specification into running, self-healing pods. It's the group deciding how Deployments roll out, how Jobs retry, how DaemonSets place a pod per node. JK: Adding to what Maciej described, as the industry shifts, we are seeing a massive demand to run complex, non-traditional workloads like distributed AI training, batch computing, and dynamic agent environments. Our role is expanding: we aren't just maintaining the classic workloads API, but we are actively evolving it and establishing new patterns (like the Agent Sandbox) to make sure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. NF: Looking at the workload APIs owned by SIG Apps (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs), which areas are receiving the most attention from maintainers and contributors? MS: After a long stretch focused on making batch workloads run smoothly on Kubernetes, we’ve shifted attention to make sure serving workloads (DaemonSets, StatefulSets, etc) aren’t left behind. This means performance and high-scale improvements to rollout and scaling behavior, plus working through our backlog of user-reported issues, prioritizing the ones with the strongest support from the user base. Current focus areasAs Kubernetes workloads grow in scale and complexity, the challenges facing workload controllers evolve as well. We asked the SIG Apps chairs where contributors are focusing their efforts today and which resilience problems they believe are the highest priorities. NF: From your perspective, what are the most important workload resilience problems SIG Apps is trying to solve today? MS: Node lifecycle challenges have come up repeatedly across SIG Apps, SIG Node, and SIG Autoscaling discussions. DaemonSets and Jobs are just where the pain is most visible, since they're the workloads most directly bound to node state. Rather than solve it piecemeal within one SIG, we've settled on spinning up a dedicated Node Lifecycle Working Group to focus on this properly and hopefully land long-term solutions instead of one-off patches. JK: From an AI perspective, resilience is critical. When you are running a massive distributed LLM training job that spans hundreds of GPUs, a single node failure can halt the entire pipeline. Similarly, if a DaemonSet that runs your logging or GPU monitoring agent gets stuck on a bad node, it impacts the entire cluster's health. In addition to the work in the Node Lifecycle WG to handle infrastructure-level degradation, SIG Apps is addressing this at the orchestration layer through subprojects like JobSet (for distributed training) and LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) (for sharded LLM inference). These APIs introduce patterns like "all-or-nothing" failure handling, where a single pod or job failure triggers a coordinated group-level restart to resume from the last clean checkpoint, rather than letting stuck workloads hang in an inconsistent state. Real-world impactThe work happening within SIG Apps extends far beyond controller implementations and API design. We wanted to understand what these improvements mean in practice for platform teams operating Kubernetes clusters in production. NF: For platform teams operating Kubernetes in production, what practical improvements would they notice if the node lifecycle and workload resilience work currently under discussion is successfully delivered? MS: I’m mostly looking from the sidelines, the folks actually in the Node Lifecycle Working Group would give you a sharper answer. But from where I sit, I’m hoping their work translates into fewer 3am pages that turn out to be “a DaemonSet rollout got stuck because node X was flaky, and someone had to manually cordon/delete/restart to unstick it.” JK: +1 to what Maciej said, and beyond reducing manual intervention, platform teams will also see much better resource predictability and cost efficiency. For example, in AI workloads where GPU idle time is extremely expensive, having Kubernetes automatically detect a degraded node and reschedule the training coordinator or agent before the job crashes means less wasted compute and more stable job execution. Challenges and trade-offsEvolving APIs that millions of workloads rely on requires careful engineering and even more careful decision-making. We asked the SIG Apps chairs about the technical and operational trade-offs they weigh when introducing changes to Kubernetes’ core workload controllers. NF: What are some of the hardest technical or operational trade-offs SIG Apps encounters when evolving core workload controllers? MS: Honestly, a few tensions keep coming up: how aggressively a controller should give up on stuck pods, and what signals it actually needs to make that call correctly. At the same time, we always have to think about backward compatibility. Deployment, DaemonSet, and Job behavior has been depended on for a decade , so even a change that’s clearly “more correct” can break automation people built around the old behavior without meaning to. JK: One of our hardest trade-offs is resisting the urge to make "elegant" design changes that break backward compatibility. Instead, we have to design opt-in features that let users adopt new behaviors without forcing them on legacy workloads. When we need to support completely new paradigms, we prefer introducing them as CRDs first rather than bloating the core APIs, like we are doing with Agent Sandbox, JobSet, and LWS. Looking aheadWhile much of SIG Apps’ work focuses on maintaining the stability of existing workload APIs, the group is also shaping the future of Kubernetes through new enhancements and proposals. We concluded by asking about one proposal that recently returned to active development and what it represents for the future of workload management. NF: The SIG recently discussed reviving KEP-4443 with a target release of Kubernetes 1.38. What opportunities or challenges does this proposal aim to address, and why is now the right time to revisit it? KEP-4443 addresses a small but real gap in the Job API: a PodFailurePolicy can be configured to add a condition reason to the JobFailed condition, but different pod failure policy rules targeting different container exit codes all produce that same generic reason. The proposal is simple: an optional Name field on each PodFailurePolicyRule, which gets appended to the JobFailed condition reason, so higher-level tools like JobSet can finally react differently depending on which rule triggered the failure. As for timing, the answer is as simple as it always is in open source: we lost the original contributor who was driving this. Now we’ve got someone new interested in picking it up, that’s why we’re targeting the next release. Getting InvolvedNF: For someone interested in contributing to SIG Apps, where would you recommend they start, especially if they are not yet a Kubernetes maintainer? MS: The best place to start is the #sig-apps slack channel and our regular SIG Apps meetings. We’ve all started there, and if it feels intimidating, or nobody replies right away, that’s completely normal. Everyone's busy. It's not personal. JK: In addition to what Maciej answered, I'd suggest looking at our newer subprojects and initiatives. Contributing to stable APIs like Deployment or StatefulSet can be daunting because the barrier for making changes is very high due to backward compatibility, and there is much less low-hanging fruit. If you are new to the community, projects like the Agent Sandbox are fantastic entry points. They are actively evolving, have a friendly group of maintainers, and offer plenty of greenfield development opportunities where you can make a significant impact quickly. SummarySIG Apps has shaped how Kubernetes applications are deployed and operated since the project’s earliest days. While users often interact with Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, and DaemonSets without thinking about the controllers behind them, the work within SIG Apps continues to shape the reliability and scalability of workloads across the Kubernetes ecosystem. From improving workload resilience and node lifecycle behavior to enabling new patterns for AI and distributed computing, the SIG is evolving Kubernetes while remaining committed to one of the project’s core principles: preserving the stability and backward compatibility that users depend on. Whether you’re interested in core workload APIs, emerging projects like Agent Sandbox, or helping improve the operational experience of Kubernetes users everywhere, SIG Apps offers many opportunities to get involved.

title: [CNCF] From attendee badge to speaker badge: My first KubeCon at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon India 2026
summary: There is something surreal about your first KubeCon being one where you walk onto the stage as a speaker. Most people ease into this community by attending a few conferences, lurking in hallway tracks, and working up the courage to submit a CFP. I did it backward. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon India 2026 in Mumbai was my very first KubeCon + CloudNativeCon event, and I experienced it from both sides of the podium. Here is how it went. The talk: Running an AI cluster on the DGX Spark I co-presented “Run Your Own AI Cluster on a DGX Spark: Kubernetes, GPUs, and DRA” with my co-speaker, who is also my dad, Janakiram MSV. Presenting alongside him made this special on a level that goes beyond the conference itself. I grew up watching him speak at technology events. Standing next to him at the same podium, in front of the KubeCon audience, felt like a full-circle moment. The talk itself covered how we turned NVIDIA’s DGX Spark into a self-hosted AI cluster. We walked through building a Kubernetes cluster on the hardware, exposing GPUs to workloads, and using Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to schedule them properly, ending with serving models on infrastructure you fully own and control. If you missed it, the recording is up on YouTube: Run Your Own AI Cluster on a DGX Spark Speaking at a conference of this scale for the first time taught me a few things quickly. The rehearsals matter. The AV check matters. And no amount of preparation fully prepares you for looking out at a hall that size. But once we got going, the nerves faded, and it just became a conversation about technology we genuinely love working with. The Two Pins I Carried Home Somewhere between the sessions and the hallway conversations, I picked up two small pins: the blue Kubestronaut pin and its golden counterpart. The Golden Kubestronaut title means completing every CNCF certification there is. For me, that was less a trophy hunt and more a long, unglamorous grind of labs, practice environments, and a lot of weekends. I started it because I wanted my fundamentals to be real, not resume-deep. As it happens, I am the youngest person in India to complete it. I did not think much about that fact until people at the event started reacting to it, and their reactions honestly meant more than the milestone itself. If there is anything worth taking from my path, it is not the record. It is that the entire journey ran on things this community built and gave away for free: open documentation, community-run study groups, and platforms like KodeKloud. The pins are just a small, physical reminder of that. The People: Why KubeCon is really about the Hallway Track Everyone tells you that the real value of KubeCon is the people. I can now confirm this firsthand. Saiyam Pathak was one of the highlights of the entire event for me. After spending real time with him across the conference, I came away having made a genuine friend in the community. He is exactly as generous and energetic in person as his content suggests. Mumshad Mannambeth, founder of KodeKloud, was another meeting I will not forget. KodeKloud’s labs were a core part of my certification journey, so getting to thank the person behind the platform in person and talk about where cloud native learning is headed meant a lot. During a CXO meet hosted alongside the conference, I also met Yongkang He, founder of Kubestrong. When the Golden Kubestronaut milestone came up, he insisted on capturing the moment with a photo together. Moments like that are a reminder of how much this community celebrates its own. And of course, spending the event with the Nirmata team, meeting community members at our booth, and putting faces to GitHub handles I have interacted with for over a year made the whole thing feel less like a conference and more like a reunion I had somehow never attended before. What Surprised Me as a First-Timer A few honest observations from someone who had never been to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon before: The event scale is massive, but navigable. Thousands of attendees and a massive venue may sound overwhelming, but the community is unusually approachable. Speakers, maintainers, and founders all walk the same hallways, and almost everyone is happy to talk. Being a speaker changes the experience. The speaker badge is a conversation starter. People come up to you after your talk with questions, ideas, and sometimes job leads. If you have been on the fence about submitting a CFP, this alone is worth it. India’s cloud native community is enormous and hungry. The energy in the sessions, the depth of questions, and the sheer number of students and early-career engineers in attendance made it clear that this region will shape the next decade of this ecosystem. What I Am Taking Home Beyond the badge, the pins, and the photos, I am taking home three things: Confidence. I now know I can stand on the KubeCon stage and deliver a technical talk. The next CFP will be easier to write. Relationships. The friendships and connections from this week are the kind that compound over years in this community. Momentum. Talking to people about GPUs, DRA, and AI on Kubernetes all week confirmed that this intersection is exactly where I want to be building. If you are an early-career engineer wondering whether KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is worth it, or whether your CFP idea is good enough, take this as your sign. Write the talk, submit it, and show up.
